outcome: As of 12 October 2026, 509,203 is still only conjectured to be the lowest Riesel number: 41 odd k below 509,203 have no known prime k·2ⁿ − 1 (PrimeGrid status page generated 12 Oct 2026; the same 41 values are in Wikipedia's list, revised 6 Oct 2026). Since 26 January 2024 the one dated base-2 elimination found is k = 107347 (107347·2²³⁴²⁷⁵¹⁷ − 1, proven prime, submitted 4 Aug 2024), which removes one candidate and settles nothing else. A second elimination, k = 192971, is listed as found but its date could not be recovered. No covering set for any odd k below 509,203 was found or claimed, no proof of minimality exists, and no AI system is named in any source read for this problem.
problem_asks: The bullet asks one yes/no question, Is 509,203 the lowest Riesel number?, and it presupposes that 509,203 is a Riesel number. Parts: (a) Is 509,203 a Riesel number, i.e. is 509,203·2ⁿ − 1 composite for every n ≥ 1? (b) Is there any odd k < 509,203 that is a Riesel number, i.e. with k·2ⁿ − 1 composite for every n ≥ 1? A 'no' to (b) needs one such k. A 'yes' to (b) needs every odd k < 509,203 to have some n with k·2ⁿ − 1 prime. Riesel numbers are odd positive integers; the bullet adds no further restriction.

events.what_happened: Hans Riesel, 'Några stora primtal', Elementa 39 (1956), pp. 258–260 (Swedish), shows 509203·2ⁿ − 1 is composite for all n ≥ 1, and that the same holds for 509203 + 11184810m for every m ≥ 0, using a system of congruences. This is the origin of 509203 as a Riesel number. I did not read the 1956 paper; the reference and claim come from Cowles and Gamboa (arXiv 1110.4671, Introduction and reference [6]) and from Wikipedia.
events.delivers: 509203 is a Riesel number, and so is every member of the progression 509203 + 11184810m (m ≥ 0), which gives infinitely many Riesel numbers. It says nothing about whether any odd k < 509,203 is Riesel.
events.remains: Whether any odd k < 509,203 is a Riesel number. That is all of part (b) of problem_asks.
events.time_since_posted: About 70 years. Later work uses the result (Cowles and Gamboa 2011; the Wikipedia article; OEIS A101036), but I found no referee or re-derivation of the 1956 congruences in the sources I read.
events.directly_checkable: Yes, for 509203 itself, through the cover {3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 241}, which appears in the 2011 ACL2 paper and OEIS A345685. See the event acl2-2011 for the residue argument.
events.direction: Cuts for 509203 being a Riesel number (it is). Silent on minimality.
events.object: The number 509203 with its congruence structure: a finite list of congruence conditions on the exponent (via a cover) under which 509203·2ⁿ − 1 is always composite. Constructive; the 1956 congruences were not read.

events.what_happened: Filaseta, Finch and Kozek, 'On powers associated with Sierpiński numbers, Riesel numbers and Polignac's conjecture'. The publication details (J. Number Theory 2008, pp. 1916–1940) come from a search summary and were not confirmed on the Erdős page, which cites [FFK08] without a journal or year. Per OEIS A101036 (comments by Nielsen, 2019, and Fröhlich, 2019), Theorem 11 of this paper gives a Riesel number thought to lack a covering set, and the paper conjectures infinitely many Riesel numbers without covering systems (OEIS cites page 16). I could not read the paper: the Whittier draft returned as undecodable binary.
events.delivers: Per secondhand reports only: a Riesel-number candidate (Theorem 11) that may lack a covering set, and a conjecture that infinitely many Riesel numbers lack covering systems. The paper concerns the covering method for Riesel numbers. It says nothing about odd k < 509,203 being Riesel.
events.time_since_posted: About 18 years. Cited by OEIS A101036 (2019) and by the Erdős #1113 page (last updated 29 Dec 2025, which cites [FFK08]).
events.doubts: The OEIS comments on the Theorem 11 candidate are conditional ('if the Riesel number mentioned ... does in fact not have a covering set'), so whether it lacks a covering set is not established in the sources I read.
events.direction: Concerns whether some Riesel numbers arise from covering systems. Cuts against the covering method as a complete account of Riesel numbers, not against 509,203 being the lowest.
events.object: Per OEIS only: a Riesel number (Theorem 11) said to lack a covering set, and a conditional related candidate (a squared 49-digit integer) noted against sequence A076337. Neither was read in the source. Whether it is explicit is not established.

events.what_happened: John R. Cowles and Ruben Gamboa, 'Verifying Sierpiński and Riesel Numbers in ACL2', arXiv:1110.4671, submitted 21 Oct 2011; EPTCS 70 (ACL2 2011 workshop), pp. 20–27. Gives ACL2 macros that take a Riesel or Sierpiński candidate and its cover and generate proof events showing that every term of the infinite family has a smaller factor in the cover. The Introduction says 'H. Riesel [6] showed 509203 is a Riesel number with cover (3 5 7 13 17 241)'. Appendix A, 'Smallest known Riesel number', lists k = 509203 with that cover. Read from the readable ar5iv HTML; the arXiv PDF returned as binary.
events.delivers: Mechanical verification, in ACL2, of the covering-set method for Sierpiński and Riesel candidates. The readable text puts 509203 with cover (3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 241) and calls it the smallest known Riesel number. Whether the ACL2 development contains a complete proof event for k = 509203 was not confirmed from the readable text. The result establishes the Riesel property of 509203, not minimality.
events.remains: All of part (b) of problem_asks. The paper contains no statement about odd k < 509,203.

events.directly_checkable: Yes. With cover (3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 241) every n ≥ 1 is caught by a prime: 3 catches even n; 5 catches n ≡ 1 (mod 4); 7 catches n ≡ 2 (mod 3); 13 catches n ≡ 7 (mod 12); 17 catches n ≡ 7 (mod 8); 241 catches n ≡ 3 (mod 24). Residues of 509203 are 1 mod 3, 3 mod 5, 2 mod 7, 6 mod 13, 2 mod 17, and 211 mod 241. Each k·2ⁿ − 1 exceeds 241, so each term is composite. I checked this by hand; the machine check was not run.
events.direction: Supports 509203 being a Riesel number. No bearing on whether a smaller odd k is Riesel.
events.object: The cover (3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 241) for k = 509203: six primes such that every 509203·2ⁿ − 1 (n ≥ 1) is divisible by one of them, so 509203 is a Riesel number. Explicit, a finite residue check over n mod 24.

events.what_happened: Bispels, Cohen, Harrington, Lowrance, Pontes, Schaumann and Wong, 'On Sierpiński and Riesel Repdigits and Repintegers', arXiv:2505.00778, v1 1 May 2025, v2 24 Jul 2025; journal reference INTEGERS 26 (2026), A12. The paper studies whether Sierpiński and Riesel numbers can be b-repdigits or b-repunits. It uses 509203 in two places: 'To date, 509203 is the smallest known Riesel number', and Theorem 3.4, which gives a bound κ′ ≤ 509203 for a repdigit-related quantity, recalled as 'the smallest known Riesel number'. It does not claim minimality, and the paper does not use the term 'Riesel problem'.

events.delivers: For repdigit and repunit forms of the Sierpiński and Riesel problems: bounds on repdigit-related quantities, and which such forms the covering method can or cannot reach (full text read: Theorems 3.4 and 3.5, Table 1). It takes 509203 as the smallest known Riesel number. Nothing it delivers is a statement about odd k < 509,203 being Riesel.

summary:
Sources read: Wikipedia's Riesel number article (last edited 6 Oct 2026); PrimeGrid's Riesel status page (generated 12 Oct 2026); OEIS A101036, A050412, A101050 and A108129 (last modified 12 Oct 2026); PrimePages record 107347·2^23427517−1 (t5k id 138376); arXiv 1110.4671 (ACL2, via ar5iv) and arXiv 2505.00778 (full HTML); ProofWiki's historical note (24 Feb 2021 snapshot); Wikiversity's Riesel conjectures table; the Erdős #1113 page; openai/math (README, lean folder, preprints listing, CONTENTS.md read in pages). Rieselprime.de pages (Riesel_problem_1, Riesel_Sieve, the k = 2293, 192971 and base-5 pages) returned 503 on every fetch attempt, so their content is taken from search snippets, and each such date is marked as not opened.

Status. 509,203 is a Riesel number (Riesel 1956; cover {3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 241} from the 2011 ACL2 paper, which I checked by hand). Whether it is the lowest rests on 41 odd k below 509,203 for which no prime k·2ⁿ − 1 is known. Every source that gives a current list gives the same 41 values, and I found no covering set for any of them. Wikipedia and OEIS both describe 509,203 as conjectured minimal. I did not verify that every other odd k below 509,203 is excluded by a covering set or a small prime, but the sources describe the 41 as the unresolved remainder of a candidate list, which is how I have read them.

What happened in the window (after 26 Jan 2024). Three events. (1) The Brown result (OEIS, 31 Jul / 1 Aug 2024) fixes the least exponent for k = 104917; 104917 was already non-Riesel from a 1999 prime, so this is discounted for scope. (2) The 107347 prime (submitted 4 Aug 2024) eliminates one candidate. Under §2.1 a single case settled counts, so I record it as an event and do not weigh it. (3) arXiv 2505.00778 (May 2025) on repdigit Riesel numbers uses 509203 as the smallest known Riesel number. It does not make a minimality claim and its bound κ′ ≤ 509203 concerns a different quantity, so it is discounted. Also in the window: base-5 eliminations (2024, 2025), which concern a neighbouring problem.

Close calls. (i) The 192971 elimination has no recoverable date. If it falls after 26 Jan 2024, the window holds two base-2 eliminations, not one; I could not settle this. (ii) The 41 open values were the same on Wikipedia and on PrimeGrid, so nothing in the sources shows a change since August 2024; the list has been constant across the sources I read. (iii) Whether the Brown OEIS result counts as 'in scope' is a yes/no on whether 104917 was a candidate. It was not, since its prime dates from 1999.

AI. No source for this problem names an AI system. I searched the Riesel problem with AI terms (AI, LLM, GPT, Claude, Gemini, AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, OpenAI, DeepMind, Anthropic, Lean formalisation) and checked the places AI results are collected: the openai/math repository (its README says the vast majority of its roughly 720 manuscripts came from an unreleased internal OpenAI model; the visible index entries I read, roughly 001 to 377 of about 719, contain no Riesel, Sierpiński or covering-set entry, but the preprints folder listing is truncated at 100 of about 719 names, so the search there is incomplete), Tao's AI-contributions tracker (which covers Erdős problems; I did not search it for Riesel), and the Epoch and Erdős trackers (no Riesel item). Two unrelated AI results surfaced: Anthropic's Riemann-hypothesis preprint (press reports; year not confirmed) and OpenAI's manuscript release (Oct 2026). Neither concerns Riesel numbers as far as the search shows. Every AI-related claim in this record is a negative finding, and the openai/math gap is the main open risk.
competing_reading: The strongest case for reading the window as active: PrimeGrid is searching all 41 remaining k at n up to about 17.1 million (the status page's 'max in progress'), a 7-million-digit proven prime eliminated a candidate in August 2024, and if 192971 was found after 26 Jan 2024 the window holds two eliminations, so the minimality question is advancing. Against that: the open list is the same in every current source, the only dated in-window base-2 elimination is one candidate of 41, and nothing in the window bears on a smaller odd k being Riesel. On the record as it stands, nothing in the window changes whether 509,203 is the lowest Riesel number.
what_would_settle_it: For the minimality question: a prime k·2ⁿ − 1 for each of the 41 open k-values (which would make 509,203 the lowest Riesel number, given that the sources describe the 41 as the entire unresolved remainder), or a covering set for any one of them (which would make that k a Riesel number below 509,203 and refute minimality). For the window: the discovery date and finder of 192971·2¹⁴⁷⁷³⁴⁹⁸ − 1 (the Prime-Wiki k = 192971 page, or its PrimePages entry), and the PrimeGrid Riesel_problem_1 and Riesel_Sieve pages once they serve again. For the AI question: the openai/math index entries beyond roughly 377 and the full preprints listing, searched for Riesel, Sierpiński and covering-set titles. For the 1956 result: Riesel's Elementa note itself, which I did not read.

events.credibility_reason: Not established whether the number is a proven prime or only a probable prime.

judgement.why: The statement asks whether 509,203 is the least Riesel number; a yes needs a prime for every remaining odd k below it, a no needs a covering set (or other proof) for one. The base-2 prime discoveries each eliminate one of finitely many candidates by exhibiting a single prime: these are finite checks that narrow where a smaller Riesel number could hide without settling the question, so I scored them instances, including the only dated in-window one (107347, Aug 2024). The close call was case versus instances for these: one could read each k as a restriction, but a single prime found by search is exactly the finite-certificate pattern F5 describes, and 41 candidates remain. Riesel 1956 establishes the statement's presupposition (509,203 is Riesel) via a hand-checkable cover, scored case/checkable as a witness; it is pre-snapshot and cannot make the problem open_stale. The ACL2 paper formalises a known result (none). Brown's least-exponent computation for 104917, the repdigit paper, FFK's covering-free Riesel numbers, and the base-5 eliminations all answer different questions (variant). No AI system is credited anywhere.
judgement.doubts: The 192971 elimination has no recoverable date, so it is left unplaced; under either scope reading it would not change the problem's status. The AI negative rests on an incomplete scan of the openai/math index (entries beyond ~377 unsearched). Several pre-2024 dates and primality statuses come from snippets only.
